## Retirement Announcement and Public Response

### Coordinating with Air France

BA initially sought to coordinate its Concorde retirement with Air France, wanting both to retire at the same time. BA preferred October (end of summer schedule), but Air France declined to delay and announced their retirement for May 2003, just weeks away. This reflected fundamentally different attitudes between the airlines, with French sentiment making any celebratory dual retirement impossible in the shadow of the accident.

### The Announcement

BA chose an extraordinary meeting of "Forum 150" (top 150 managers) on 9th April 2003 to announce the retirement, followed by a public release. Bannister suggested switching to 10th April when he noted that the 9th marked the 34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight—bad optics for announcing an ending on that date.

When the announcement came, it triggered what Bannister calls the "Marmite factor": roughly two-thirds of senior management expressed great sadness, while the remainder felt relief. No one was ambivalent.

### The Official Line

At the press conference, when asked why Concorde was being retired, Bannister found himself searching for a simple expression. He answered: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons"—a phrase that became universally adopted as the party line, even though internally he had long felt it was "quite the wrong decision at the wrong time for the wrong reasons."

### Branson Question

The persistent question about allowing Richard Branson to take the aircraft required careful handling. BA anticipated that whatever the outcome, Branson would spin it to his advantage. The official response was that ownership decisions weren't BA's to make since the UK government originally funded the aircraft. At a Guild of Air Pilots event, a senior Virgin pilot told Bannister they'd never really wanted it—"it would probably send us bust!"—which Bannister believed was likely true.

### Single Aircraft for Air Shows

Retention of one Concorde for air shows was impractical. Unlike the Vulcan (which operates on a "Permit to Fly" with lower certification standards), Concorde required a full "Certificate of Airworthiness" and "Type Certificate." The £60 million per annum infrastructure cost was set to rise by another £40 million—and this cost didn't scale down with fleet reduction. Even at £50 million annually, it would be "a million a week" for one aircraft. Airbus, focused on the approaching A380 and successful A320 family, had no interest in retaining the Type Certificate, and was under no compulsion to transfer it. The technology in Concorde's air-intake computers remained proprietary and relevant to current military aircraft.

### Shift to Celebration

As spring turned to summer, public discussion shifted from questioning the decision to celebrating Concorde's legacy. People began talking about "the wonderful job UK plc had done" in accomplishing what the Americans hadn't. Bannister overheard conversations like: "I never got to fly on Concorde myself, sadly, but I know someone whose Aunt Mabel once flew on it and she'd had the time of her life."

Even though Concorde was a common sight over London—taking off or landing six to eight times daily with Olympuses crackling overhead—people still stopped and looked up, knowing the end approached.

Author Edward de Bono told Bannister that Concorde appealed to both sides of the brain: the analytical and the artistic, being "technologically superb and artistically graceful." For Bannister, however, the reason was simpler: most Brits had come to feel "a sense of ownership"—that's my Concorde up there.

## 39

It didn’t take long for the retirement-as-celebration idea to gain traction. The next question was how to deliver it. We needed to signal to Air France that we wanted to coordinate, initially agreeing to retire simultaneously at season's end in October. Air France then chose May—just weeks away—reflecting their different attitude; in the shadow of the accident, there was never any prospect in France that a dual retirement perceived as celebratory would be sanctioned. With each airline going its own way, the announcement strategy required careful timing.

BA's internal 'Forum 150' network—briefing the top 150 managers by the CEO—was selected for 9th April 2003. I pointed out this was the 34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight. We switched to the 10th. When the day arrived, I wore uniform to signal gravitas, presenting the rehearsed rationale via slide show.

We hit the Marmite factor: roughly two-thirds of senior management expressed sadness, the remainder relief—no ambivalence, which presaged the public reaction. Still in uniform, I became company spokesman. For customers, we stressed this was a commercial decision spurred by factors beyond control, promising continued service via upgraded Club Class and First on 747s.

Having argued internally that Concorde shouldn't retire, I accepted the role because I could demonstrate collective responsibility and help retire the aircraft with the dignity she deserved—a celebration, not a wake.

Facing TV lights at the press conference was hard. When asked why she was being retired, I hesitated, then: 'It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons.' I had no idea where the words came from, but they became the universal party line.

The persistent question: why not give Concorde to Richard Branson? We'd anticipated this. If Branson succeeded, he'd say BA couldn't run a tea shop; if he failed, he'd blame BA's maintenance; if we refused, we'd be beastly. Our response—government funding meant transfer wasn't our decision—was a cop-out with enough truth to carry the day. A senior Virgin pilot later confirmed they'd have gone bust.

Another common question: couldn't one aircraft be retained for air shows? This had worked for the Lancaster, Spitfires, and Avro Vulcan—flown under a 'Permit to Fly' with lower certification standards for non-passenger aircraft. Concorde required a 'Certificate of Airworthiness' and 'Type Certificate', far higher standards. To maintain certification for air shows meant retaining both, requiring money—lots of it.

The infrastructure cost was fixed: £60 million per annum, soon rising by another £40 million, whether operating seven aircraft or one. Even halved to £50 million, that's a million pounds per week for a single aircraft. Beyond cost, someone had to maintain it. A Type Certificate Holder—normally the manufacturer—was required for engineering. Airbus, focused on the approaching A380 and successful A320 family, had no interest; they had no compulsion to transfer it, and it was in their interest not to, as Concorde's air-intake computer technology controlling engine airflow was proprietary and still used on military aircraft. No other realistic candidate existed, and at air shows no one would credit Airbus anyway.

After spring's questioning storm, discussion drifted toward Concorde's legacy. People discussed UK's achievement, the 'wonderful job' of doing what the Americans hadn't. I overheard: 'I never flew on Concorde, but my Aunt Mabel did and she had the time of her life.' The clamour for a celebration eclipsed the doom-merchants. BA ensured recognition not just for the aircraft but for everyone who'd designed, built, brought her into service, operated, maintained—flight crew, cabin crew, engineers, baggage handlers, ticket agents—and the public, traveller and non-traveller alike.

When Concorde roared overhead six to eight times daily, Londoners stopped and looked up—they always had, but more now, knowing it would end. Edward de Bono said she appealed to both brain hemispheres: technologically superb yet artistically graceful. For me the reason was simpler: most Brits felt individual ownership. That's my Concorde up there—something to be rightly proud of.

Edward de Bono observed she appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically sophisticated yet artistically graceful. For most Britons, the connection ran deeper: they felt individual pride in her presence overhead. The public discussion shifted toward celebrating Concorde's legacy rather than mourning her departure. People recognized the achievement—what the UK had accomplished, doing what the Americans couldn't. The demand for recognition extended beyond the aircraft itself to encompass everyone involved: designers, builders, operators, maintenance crews, flight and cabin staff, engineers, baggage handlers, and ticket agents.
